merge.title.githubRefused.text: GitHub refused the merge. Homeroom tries again at {{time}}.
merge.title.githubRefused.description: Tooltip on the "Waiting on GitHub" status badge of a proposal whose merge GitHub refused for a reason nobody has to act on. {{time}} is a clock time such as 10:45, shown in the viewer's own time zone. "Homeroom" is the name of the platform and stays as it is.

merge.title.githubRefusedSoon.text: GitHub refused the merge. Homeroom tries again in a few minutes.
merge.title.githubRefusedSoon.description: Tooltip on the "Waiting on GitHub" status badge of a proposal whose merge GitHub refused for a reason nobody has to act on, when the next try's time has passed or was not recorded. "Homeroom" is the name of the platform and stays as it is.

merge.title.githubChecks.text: GitHub is building and scanning the release images for this change, which usually takes about 6 minutes. It merges as soon as they pass.
merge.title.githubChecks.description: Tooltip on the "Waiting on GitHub" status badge of a proposal whose merge waits for the required checks GitHub runs on it. "GitHub" is a product name and stays as it is.

merge.status.goingLive.description: Status badge on a proposal that has been merged while the live app is still being updated to run it. Shown with a spinner.

merge.title.goingLive.text: This change is merged. Production is being updated to run it.
merge.title.goingLive.description: Tooltip on the "Going live…" status badge of a proposal. "change" is a noun: the proposed change. Production is the live app people use.

merge.status.merged.description: Status badge on a proposal that is finished: its change is now part of the app. Shown after a check mark.

merge.status.merging.description: Status badge on a proposal whose change is being merged into the app right now. Shown with a spinner.

merge.title.merging.text: This change is being merged into the app and production is rebuilding.
merge.title.merging.description: Tooltip on the "Merging…" status badge of a proposal. "change" is a noun: the proposed change. Production is the live app people use.

merge.status.resolving.description: Status badge on a proposal: the platform is reconciling it with the app's latest code by itself. Shown with a spinner.

merge.title.resolving.text: Reconciling conflicts with main automatically, then retrying the merge.
merge.title.resolving.description: Tooltip on the "Resolving conflicts automatically…" status badge of a proposal. "main" is the name of the app's main code branch and stays as it is.

merge.status.conflictFailed.description: Status badge on a proposal, shown after a warning sign: the platform tried to reconcile it with the app's latest code and could not.

merge.title.conflictFailed.text: The last automatic conflict resolution failed. The owner needs to resolve manually.
merge.title.conflictFailed.description: Tooltip on the "Conflict resolution failed" status badge of a proposal. The owner is the person who made the proposal.

merge.status.mergeConflict.description: Status badge on a proposal, shown after a warning sign: merging it was tried and failed because it conflicts with the app's latest code.

merge.title.mergeConflict.text: Going live was attempted but this change conflicts with main. The change’s creator needs to bring it up to date from the change’s page ("Sync with main").
merge.title.mergeConflict.description: Tooltip on the "Merge failed: conflict" status badge of a proposal. "change" is a noun: the proposed change. "main" is the app's main code branch and stays as it is; "Sync with main" is the name of a button on the change's page.

merge.status.conflictsWithMain.description: Status badge on a proposal, shown after a warning sign: it can no longer be merged as it stands because the app's main code has changed. "Conflicts" is a verb (this proposal conflicts); "main" is the main code branch and stays as it is.

merge.status.conflictsWithMainFiles_one.description: Status badge on a proposal, shown after a warning sign: it conflicts with the app's main code. {{count}} is the number of files in conflict, shown bare after a middle dot. "Conflicts" is a verb; "main" stays as it is.

merge.status.conflictsWithMainFiles_othe.description: Status badge on a proposal, shown after a warning sign: it conflicts with the app's main code. {{count}} is the number of files in conflict, shown bare after a middle dot. "Conflicts" is a verb; "main" stays as it is.

merge.title.conflictUnresolvable.text: Main has moved on and this proposal no longer merges on its own. The platform tried to resolve it and could not. The change’s creator needs to bring it up to date from the change’s page ("Sync with main").
merge.title.conflictUnresolvable.description: Tooltip on the "Conflicts with main" status badge of a proposal, when the platform's own attempt to fix the conflict failed. "Main"/"main" is the app's main code branch; "Sync with main" is the name of a button on the change's page.

merge.title.conflictForkHead.text: Main has moved on and this proposal no longer merges on its own. Its branch lives on the creator’s own fork, which the platform cannot write to, so only the creator can bring it up to date.
merge.title.conflictForkHead.description: Tooltip on the "Conflicts with main" status badge of a proposal whose code lives in its creator's own copy (fork) of the repository. "Main" is the app's main code branch.

merge.title.conflictAwaitingApproval.text: Main has moved on and this proposal no longer merges on its own. The platform resolves it once the vote passes. The creator can bring it up to date sooner from the change’s page ("Sync with main").
merge.title.conflictAwaitingApproval.description: Tooltip on the "Conflicts with main" status badge of a proposal that is still being voted on. "Main"/"main" is the app's main code branch; "Sync with main" is the name of a button on the change's page.

merge.title.conflictChecksFailing.text: Main has moved on and this proposal no longer merges on its own. Its checks are failing too, so the platform does not resolve the conflict yet: the change’s creator fixes the checks first, and then the platform resolves the conflict.
merge.title.conflictChecksFailing.description: Tooltip on the "Conflicts with main" status badge of a proposal whose automated checks are failing as well. "Main" is the app's main code branch.

merge.title.conflictChecksError.text: Main has moved on and this proposal no longer merges on its own. Its checks could not run, so the platform does not resolve the conflict yet: once they are re-run and pass, the platform resolves the conflict.
merge.title.conflictChecksError.description: Tooltip on the "Conflicts with main" status badge of a proposal whose automated checks could not run (the test run itself failed). "Main" is the app's main code branch.

merge.title.conflictAutomatic.text: Main has moved on and this proposal no longer merges on its own. The platform resolves it automatically. The creator can also bring it up to date from the change’s page ("Sync with main").
merge.title.conflictAutomatic.description: Tooltip on the "Conflicts with main" status badge of a proposal, in the ordinary case where the platform will fix the conflict itself. "Main"/"main" is the app's main code branch; "Sync with main" is the name of a button on the change's page.

merge.status.previewFailed.description: Status badge on a proposal, shown after a warning sign: the test copy of the app built from this proposal (its preview) failed to start.

merge.title.previewFailedReason.text: The preview failed to start, so it can’t be tested. It can’t go live until it starts. Reason: {{reason}}
merge.title.previewFailedReason.description: Tooltip on the "Preview won't boot" status badge of a proposal. {{reason}} is the error the server recorded, in English, shown as it is.

merge.title.previewFailed.text: The preview failed to start, so it couldn’t be tested. It can’t go live until it starts.
merge.title.previewFailed.description: Tooltip on the "Preview won't boot" status badge of a proposal, when no error detail was recorded. The preview is the test copy of the app built from the proposal.

merge.status.checksWillRetry.description: Status badge on a proposal, with a spinner: its automated checks (tests) were interrupted and will be run again without anyone acting.

merge.title.checksWillRetryDetail.text: {{detail}} Merge is blocked until they pass.
merge.title.checksWillRetryDetail.description: Tooltip on the "Checks will run again" status badge of a proposal. {{detail}} is a complete sentence from the server saying why the checks are being run again; "they" are the checks.

merge.title.checksWillRetry.text: Merge is blocked until they pass.
merge.title.checksWillRetry.description: Tooltip on the "Checks will run again" status badge of a proposal, when the server gave no detail. "they" are the proposal's automated checks.

merge.status.checksError.description: Status badge on a proposal, shown after a warning sign: its automated checks (tests) ended without a result.

merge.title.checksErrorReason.text: The automated check run ended before it produced a verdict. Merge is blocked. Reason: {{reason}}
merge.title.checksErrorReason.description: Tooltip on the "Checks couldn't run" status badge of a proposal. {{reason}} is the error the server recorded, in English, shown as it is.

merge.title.checksError.text: The automated check run ended before it produced a verdict. The preview may still be available; merge is blocked until checks complete.
merge.title.checksError.description: Tooltip on the "Checks couldn't run" status badge of a proposal, when no error detail was recorded. The preview is the test copy of the app built from the proposal.

merge.status.checksFailing.description: Status badge on a proposal, shown after a warning sign: its automated checks (tests) are not passing.

merge.status.checksFailingCount_one.description: Status badge on a proposal, shown after a warning sign: its automated checks are not passing. {{count}} is how many checks fail, shown bare after a middle dot.

merge.status.checksFailingCount_other.description: Status badge on a proposal, shown after a warning sign: its automated checks are not passing. {{count}} is how many checks fail, shown bare after a middle dot.

merge.title.checksFailing.text: Checks are not passing on the preview. It can’t go live until they pass.
merge.title.checksFailing.description: Tooltip on the "Checks failing" status badge of a proposal. The preview is the test copy of the app built from the proposal; "It" is the proposal.

merge.status.checksDeferred.description: Status badge on a proposal: its automated checks (tests) have been put off, because the proposal conflicts with the app's latest code.

merge.title.checksDeferred.text: This proposal conflicts with main, so its preview was built but its tests were not run: they would judge a tree that cannot merge. They run automatically once it merges cleanly.
merge.title.checksDeferred.description: Tooltip on the "Checks deferred" status badge of a proposal. "main" is the app's main code branch and stays as it is; "a tree" is the proposal's set of code files.

merge.status.checksQueued.description: Status badge on a proposal, with a spinner: its automated checks (tests) are waiting in a queue to start, position unknown.

merge.status.checksQueuedNext.description: Status badge on a proposal, with a spinner: its automated checks are waiting in a queue and are the next to start.

merge.status.checksQueuedAhead_one.description: Status badge on a proposal, with a spinner: its automated checks are waiting in a queue. {{count}} is how many other proposals' checks run before these.

merge.status.checksQueuedAhead_other.description: Status badge on a proposal, with a spinner: its automated checks are waiting in a queue. {{count}} is how many other proposals' checks run before these.

merge.title.checksQueued.text: The preview is up, and its checks are waiting for a slot: Homeroom runs a few proposals’ checks at a time. They start on their own. It can’t go live until they pass.
merge.title.checksQueued.description: Tooltip on the "Checks waiting" status badge of a proposal. The preview is the test copy of the app built from the proposal. Homeroom is the product's name.

merge.status.checksRunning.description: Status badge on a proposal, with a spinner: its automated checks (tests) are running and started less than a minute ago.

merge.status.checksRunningFor_one.description: Status badge on a proposal, with a spinner: its automated checks are running. {{count}} is how many minutes they have been running; "min" abbreviates minutes.

merge.status.checksRunningFor_other.description: Status badge on a proposal, with a spinner: its automated checks are running. {{count}} is how many minutes they have been running; "min" abbreviates minutes.

merge.title.checksRunning.text: Still testing the preview. It can’t go live until the checks pass.
merge.title.checksRunning.description: Tooltip on the "Checks running" status badge of a proposal. The preview is the test copy of the app built from the proposal; "It" is the proposal.

merge.status.checksStarting.description: Status badge on a proposal, with a spinner: its preview is still being built and its automated checks have not begun.

merge.title.checksStarting.text: The preview is being prepared and testing is about to start. It can’t go live until the checks pass.
merge.title.checksStarting.description: Tooltip on the "Checks starting…" status badge of a proposal. The preview is the test copy of the app built from the proposal; "It" is the proposal.

merge.status.checksSkipped.description: Status badge on a proposal: its automated checks were not run because there was nothing to test. This does not block it.

merge.title.checksSkippedReason.text: Checks were skipped: {{reason}}. It can still go live.
merge.title.checksSkippedReason.description: Tooltip on the "Checks skipped" status badge of a proposal. {{reason}} is the server's reason, in English, a clause without a full stop. "It" is the proposal.

merge.title.checksSkipped.text: Checks were skipped: there was nothing to test. It can still go live.
merge.title.checksSkipped.description: Tooltip on the "Checks skipped" status badge of a proposal, when the server recorded no reason. "It" is the proposal.

merge.status.behind.description: Status badge on a proposal: the app's main code has changed since the proposal was made, though it still merges. "main" is the main code branch and stays as it is.

merge.status.behindCount_one.description: Status badge on a proposal: the app's main code has changed since the proposal was made. {{count}} is how many commits main has gained, shown bare after a middle dot. "main" stays as it is.

merge.status.behindCount_other.description: Status badge on a proposal: the app's main code has changed since the proposal was made. {{count}} is how many commits main has gained, shown bare after a middle dot. "main" stays as it is.

merge.title.behind.text: Main has moved on since this was proposed, but this still merges cleanly. Nothing needs syncing: it merges as it stands once the vote passes.
merge.title.behind.description: Tooltip on the "Behind main" status badge of a proposal. "Main" is the app's main code branch; "this" is the proposal.

merge.status.awaitingAdmin.description: Status badge on a proposal that has enough votes but, because the app is locked, still needs an admin to vote Yes.

merge.title.awaitingAdmin.text: App is locked, so it also needs at least one admin yes before it merges.
merge.title.awaitingAdmin.description: Tooltip on the "Awaiting admin approval" status badge of a proposal. "it" is the proposal; "admin yes" is a Yes vote from one of the app's admins.

merge.status.awaitingMember.description: Status badge on a proposal that has enough votes, but none from a member other than its author, which this kind of change requires. "Yes" is the name of the approving vote and keeps its capital.

merge.status.mainPaused.description: Status badge on a proposal that passed its vote and checks, while the app has stopped accepting merges because its own tests are failing.

merge.title.mainPausedNote.text: Approved and checks passed, but {{reason}}. Nothing about this change is wrong; it goes live once the app is healthy again or an admin resumes.
merge.title.mainPausedNote.description: Tooltip on the "Approved, going live is paused" status badge of a proposal. {{reason}} is the server's clause, in English, saying why the app's merges are paused; it starts lower case and has no full stop. "change" is a noun: the proposed change.

merge.title.mainPaused.text: Approved and checks passed, but main’s unit suite is failing and going live is paused for this app. Nothing about this change is wrong; it goes live once the app is healthy again or an admin resumes.
merge.title.mainPaused.description: Tooltip on the "Approved, going live is paused" status badge of a proposal, when the server gave no reason of its own. "main" is the app's main code branch; its unit suite is its set of automated tests. "change" is a noun: the proposed change.

merge.status.ready.description: Status badge on a proposal that passed its vote and its checks and is queued to be merged into the app.

merge.title.ready.text: Approved and checks passed. It goes live shortly.
merge.title.ready.description: Tooltip on the "Approved, going live shortly" status badge of a proposal. "It" is the proposal.

merge.status.waitingForYourApproval.description: Status badge on a proposal in a project that only the viewer belongs to: their own Yes vote is the one it needs.

merge.status.waitingForApproval.description: Status badge on a proposal that has been put up for a vote and does not have enough Yes votes yet.

merge.title.explicitApprovalNoTimer.text: {{requirement}} It won’t merge on a timer: it needs real Yes votes to reach the app’s normal threshold.
merge.title.explicitApprovalNoTimer.description: Tooltip on the "Waiting for approval" status badge of a proposal that changes a protected setting. {{requirement}} is a complete sentence, already translated, such as "Changes to who runs this app need a Yes from another member." "It" is the proposal; "Yes" is the name of the approving vote.

merge.status.checksPassed.description: Status badge, after a check mark, on a change still being drafted (not yet put up for a vote) whose automated checks all passed.

merge.title.checksPassed.text: Checks passed on the preview. It is ready to send for approval.
merge.title.checksPassed.description: Tooltip on the "Checks passed" status badge of a draft change. The preview is the test copy of the app built from it; "It" is the change.

merge.status.draft.description: Status badge on a change that is still being built and has not been put up for a vote. A noun.

merge.pill.statusWithTally.description: Status pill in the header of a change that is up for a vote. {{status}} is the whole status phrase, already translated ("Waiting for approval"); {{yes}} is the number of Yes votes so far and {{required}} the number needed, shown as a fraction.

merge.pill.advisoryVotes_one.text: {{count}} advisory vote from non-approvers. They don’t count toward merging
merge.pill.advisoryVotes_one.description: Tooltip on the small "+N" beside a proposal's vote tally, on an app where only invited approvers' votes count. {{count}} is the number of Yes votes cast by people who are not approvers. No full stop at the end.

merge.pill.advisoryVotes_other.text: {{count}} advisory votes from non-approvers. They don’t count toward merging
merge.pill.advisoryVotes_other.description: Tooltip on the small "+N" beside a proposal's vote tally, on an app where only invited approvers' votes count. {{count}} is the number of Yes votes cast by people who are not approvers. No full stop at the end.

venue.usernodeOpenrouter.label.description: Name of one place a change can be built: Homeroom's own servers, using AI models through the OpenRouter service. Homeroom and OpenRouter are product names; keep the middle dot.

venue.usernodeOpenrouter.blurb.text: Built on Homeroom with an OpenRouter model, on included credits or the author's own OpenRouter key.
venue.usernodeOpenrouter.blurb.description: Explains the "Homeroom · OpenRouter" venue in the tooltip of a change's card, which says where the change was built. OpenRouter is a product name; a key is an API key.

venue.usernodeClaude.label.description: Name of one place a change can be built: Homeroom's own servers, using the Claude AI model. Homeroom and Claude are product names; keep the middle dot.

venue.usernodeClaude.blurb.text: Built on Homeroom with Claude, on weekly credits or the author's own Anthropic key.
venue.usernodeClaude.blurb.description: Explains the "Homeroom · Claude" way of building a change, in menus and tooltips where a person chooses where to build. A turn is one request to the coding agent and its reply. Claude and Anthropic are names; a key is an API key.

venue.local.label.description: Name of one place a change was built: the person's own computer, where their coding agent ran the work for a change kept in Homeroom. Homeroom is the product's name; keep the middle dot.

venue.local.blurb.text: Built on the author's own machine by the Homeroom CLI, with their own Claude plan, on the same branch and proposal.
venue.local.blurb.description: Explains the "Your computer · Homeroom session" way of building a change. The Homeroom CLI is Homeroom's command-line program; a turn is one request to the coding agent and its reply; Claude is a product name.

venue.webClaudeCode.label.description: Name of one place a change can be built: Anthropic's Claude Code website. Claude Code is a product name.

venue.webClaudeCode.blurb.text: Homeroom writes the work order; Claude Code on the web builds it on your own Claude plan and pushes to your fork. Homeroom opens the pull request and imports it as a proposal. No credits, no API key.
venue.webClaudeCode.blurb.description: Explains the "Claude Code on the web" way of building a change. A fork is the person's own copy of the app's code repository on GitHub; Claude Code and Homeroom are product names.

venue.webCodex.label.description: Name of one place a change can be built: OpenAI's Codex website. Codex is a product name.

venue.webCodex.blurb.text: The same hand-off for Codex on the web and the ChatGPT plan you already pay for. Homeroom guides you through linking GitHub, forking and submitting.
venue.webCodex.blurb.description: Explains the "Codex on the web" way of building a change, listed right after "Claude Code on the web", which works the same way. Codex, ChatGPT, GitHub and Homeroom are product names.

venue.ownToolsPr.label.description: Name of one place a change can be built: the person's own computer with whatever developer tools they like, outside Homeroom. Keep the middle dot.

venue.ownToolsPr.blurb.text: Build it however you like (Cursor, Zed, vim, any agent), push a branch, then bring the pull request in with “Import Feature from a PR”.
venue.ownToolsPr.blurb.description: Explains the "Your computer · your own tools" way of building a change. "Build" is a verb. Cursor, Zed and vim are names of code editors; “Import Feature from a PR” is the name of a menu item; PR means a GitHub pull request.

venue.handoff.externalAgent.description: Names what wrote a proposal that came from a person's own computer when Homeroom does not know which coding tool it was. Shown where the tool's name (Codex, Claude Code) would be.

venue.handoff.authoredWithCodex.text: Authored with Codex on your computer.
venue.handoff.authoredWithCodex.description: Tooltip on the label that says where a session was built, for a proposal the viewer wrote on their own computer with the Codex coding tool. Codex is a product name.

venue.handoff.authoredWithClaudeCode.text: Authored with Claude Code on your computer.
venue.handoff.authoredWithClaudeCode.description: Tooltip on the label that says where a session was built, for a proposal the viewer wrote on their own computer with the Claude Code coding tool. Claude Code is a product name.

venue.handoff.authoredWithExternalAgent.text: Authored with External agent on your computer.
venue.handoff.authoredWithExternalAgent.description: Tooltip on the label that says where a session was built, for a proposal the viewer wrote on their own computer with a coding tool Homeroom cannot name.

credits.resetIn.underMinute.description: How long until the free AI credits reset, when it is less than a minute. Goes into the sentence "Free credits reset …, about {{timeLeft}} from now." as {{timeLeft}}, so it is lower case with no full stop.

credits.resetIn.minutes_one.description: How long until the free AI credits reset, in minutes, abbreviated: "45m". {{count}} is the number of minutes; "m" abbreviates minutes. Goes into the sentence "Free credits reset …, about {{timeLeft}} from now."

credits.resetIn.minutes_other.description: How long until the free AI credits reset, in minutes, abbreviated: "45m". {{count}} is the number of minutes; "m" abbreviates minutes. Goes into the sentence "Free credits reset …, about {{timeLeft}} from now."

credits.resetIn.hours_one.description: How long until the free AI credits reset, in whole hours, abbreviated: "3h". {{count}} is the number of hours; "h" abbreviates hours. Goes into the sentence "Free credits reset …, about {{timeLeft}} from now."

credits.resetIn.hours_other.description: How long until the free AI credits reset, in whole hours, abbreviated: "3h". {{count}} is the number of hours; "h" abbreviates hours. Goes into the sentence "Free credits reset …, about {{timeLeft}} from now."

credits.resetIn.hoursMinutes.description: How long until the free AI credits reset, in hours and minutes, abbreviated: "3h 20m". {{hours}} and {{minutes}} are numbers; "h" and "m" abbreviate hours and minutes. Goes into the sentence "Free credits reset …, about {{timeLeft}} from now."

credits.reset.locked.text: Connect GitHub or X to unlock $10.00/day of Homeroom credits.
credits.reset.locked.description: Shown where the reset time of the free AI credits would be, for an account that has no credits until it links a GitHub or X account. GitHub and X are product names; $10.00/day is ten US dollars a day.

credits.reset.unavailable.description: Shown where the reset time of the free AI credits would be, when Homeroom could not work out whether this account gets credits.

credits.reset.when.description: Says when the weekly free AI credits are given back, under the credit meter and in its tooltips, when the person's local time cannot be worked out. "reset" is a verb. {{when}} is the server's own name for the moment, in English, such as "Monday 00:00 UTC".

credits.reset.whenWithTimeLeft.text: Free credits reset {{when}}, about {{timeLeft}} from now.
credits.reset.whenWithTimeLeft.description: Says when the weekly free AI credits are given back and how far off that is, when the person's local time cannot be worked out. "reset" is a verb. {{when}} is the server's own name for the moment, in English, such as "Monday 00:00 UTC"; {{timeLeft}} is a short duration such as "3h 20m" or "under a minute".

credits.reset.daily.description: Says when the daily free AI credits are given back, under the credit meter and in its tooltips. "reset" is a verb. {{time}} is the time of day in the person's own clock and format, for example "9:00 AM".

credits.reset.dailyWithTimeLeft.text: Free credits reset at {{time}}, about {{timeLeft}} from now.
credits.reset.dailyWithTimeLeft.description: Says when the daily free AI credits are given back, under the credit meter and in its tooltips. "reset" is a verb. It also says how far off that is. {{time}} is the time of day in the person's own clock and format, for example "9:00 AM". {{timeLeft}} is a short duration such as "3h 20m" or "under a minute".

credits.reset.dailyUtc.description: Says when the daily free AI credits are given back, under the credit meter and in its tooltips. "reset" is a verb. This wording is for a tooltip, with the exact moment in brackets. {{time}} is the time of day in the person's own clock and format, for example "9:00 AM". {{utc}} is the same moment in UTC, already formatted, for example "Mon, Oct 5, 00:00 UTC".

credits.reset.dailyWithTimeLeftUtc.text: Free credits reset at {{time}}, about {{timeLeft}} from now ({{utc}}).
credits.reset.dailyWithTimeLeftUtc.description: Says when the daily free AI credits are given back, under the credit meter and in its tooltips. "reset" is a verb. It also says how far off that is; this wording is for a tooltip, with the exact moment in brackets. {{time}} is the time of day in the person's own clock and format, for example "9:00 AM". {{timeLeft}} is a short duration such as "3h 20m" or "under a minute". {{utc}} is the same moment in UTC, already formatted, for example "Mon, Oct 5, 00:00 UTC".

credits.reset.weekly.description: Says when the weekly free AI credits are given back, under the credit meter and in its tooltips. "reset" is a verb. {{day}} is the weekday's full name and {{time}} the time of day, both in the person's own clock and format, for example "Sunday" and "8:00 PM".

credits.reset.weeklyWithTimeLeft.text: Free credits reset {{day}} at {{time}}, about {{timeLeft}} from now.
credits.reset.weeklyWithTimeLeft.description: Says when the weekly free AI credits are given back, under the credit meter and in its tooltips. "reset" is a verb. It also says how far off that is. {{day}} is the weekday's full name and {{time}} the time of day, both in the person's own clock and format, for example "Sunday" and "8:00 PM". {{timeLeft}} is a short duration such as "3h 20m" or "under a minute".

credits.reset.weeklyUtc.description: Says when the weekly free AI credits are given back, under the credit meter and in its tooltips. "reset" is a verb. This wording is for a tooltip, with the exact moment in brackets. {{day}} is the weekday's full name and {{time}} the time of day, both in the person's own clock and format, for example "Sunday" and "8:00 PM". {{utc}} is the same moment in UTC, already formatted, for example "Mon, Oct 5, 00:00 UTC".

credits.reset.weeklyWithTimeLeftUtc.text: Free credits reset {{day}} at {{time}}, about {{timeLeft}} from now ({{utc}}).
credits.reset.weeklyWithTimeLeftUtc.description: Says when the weekly free AI credits are given back, under the credit meter and in its tooltips. "reset" is a verb. It also says how far off that is; this wording is for a tooltip, with the exact moment in brackets. {{day}} is the weekday's full name and {{time}} the time of day, both in the person's own clock and format, for example "Sunday" and "8:00 PM". {{timeLeft}} is a short duration such as "3h 20m" or "under a minute". {{utc}} is the same moment in UTC, already formatted, for example "Mon, Oct 5, 00:00 UTC".

credits.reset.atBoundary.description: Says when the daily free AI credits are given back, when the person's local time cannot be worked out. "reset" is a verb. {{boundary}} is the server's name for the moment, in English, such as "midnight UTC".

credits.reset.atBoundaryWithTimeLeft.text: Free credits reset at {{boundary}}, about {{timeLeft}} from now.
credits.reset.atBoundaryWithTimeLeft.description: Says when the daily free AI credits are given back and how far off that is, when the person's local time cannot be worked out. "reset" is a verb. {{boundary}} is the server's name for the moment, in English, such as "midnight UTC"; {{timeLeft}} is a short duration such as "3h 20m".

buildLog.stage.clone.description: Names the step of deploying an app that failed, after "Failed step:" in the "Build log" panel, which shows why an app's last deploy failed: copying the app's code repository.

buildLog.stage.build.description: Names the step of deploying an app that failed, after "Failed step:" in the "Build log" panel, which shows why an app's last deploy failed: building the app's container image. "Building" is a verb; Docker is a product name.

buildLog.stage.start.description: Names the step of deploying an app that failed, after "Failed step:" in the "Build log" panel, which shows why an app's last deploy failed: starting the app's container.

buildLog.stage.healthcheck.description: Names the step of deploying an app that failed, after "Failed step:" in the "Build log" panel, which shows why an app's last deploy failed: waiting for the started app to answer that it is healthy.

buildLog.stage.timeout.description: Stands where the failed step would be named, after "Failed step:" in the "Build log" panel, which shows why an app's last deploy failed, when the deploy took too long.

buildLog.stage.other.description: Names the step that failed, after "Failed step:" in the "Build log" panel, which shows why an app's last deploy failed, when the exact step is not known: deploying the app in general.

buildLog.empty.text: No build failure detail is recorded for this app. Failures that happened before this feature shipped weren't captured. Retry the deploy to record a fresh log.
buildLog.empty.description: Shown in the "Build log" panel of an app whose deploy failed when Homeroom kept no detail of the failure. "build" is a noun (the build of the app); "Retry" is a verb.

buildLog.meta.failedStep.description: Line in the "Build log" panel, which shows why an app's last deploy failed. <0>…</0> is the emphasised label; {{step}} names the step, for example "Building the Docker image".

buildLog.meta.whenRelative.description: Line in the "Build log" panel, which shows why an app's last deploy failed: when the failure happened. <0>…</0> is the emphasised label; {{relative}} is a short age such as "5m ago" and {{date}} the full date and time.

buildLog.meta.when.description: Line in the "Build log" panel, which shows why an app's last deploy failed: when the failure happened. <0>…</0> is the emphasised label; {{date}} is the full date and time.

buildLog.meta.commit.description: Line in the "Build log" panel, which shows why an app's last deploy failed: which commit (version of the code) was being deployed. "Commit" is a noun. <0>…</0> is the emphasised label; <1>…</1> sets the identifier in a code font; {{sha}} is the commit's short identifier.

buildLog.noLog.text: No log output was captured for this failure.
buildLog.noLog.description: Shown in the "Build log" panel of a failed deploy when the failure has a reason but no log text was saved.

buildLog.title.description: Title of the panel that shows why an app's last deploy failed. "Build" is a noun: the log of the build.

buildLog.copy.description: Button in the "Build log" panel: copies the failure's details and log text to the clipboard. "Copy" is a verb.

buildLog.copied.description: Replaces the "Copy log" button's label for a moment after the build log was copied to the clipboard.

buildLog.copyFailed.description: Replaces the "Copy log" button's label for a moment when the build log could not be copied to the clipboard.

buildLog.retry.description: Button in the "Build log" panel, for the app's creator or an admin: deploys the app again. "Retry" is a verb; "deploy" is a noun here.

buildLog.retrying.description: Replaces the "Retry deploy" button's label while the request to deploy the app again is being sent.

buildLog.retryFailed.description: Toast shown when the request to deploy an app again was refused and the server gave no message. {{status}} is the HTTP status number, such as 500.

buildLog.ago.justNow.description: How long ago an app's deploy failed, in the "When:" line of the "Build log" panel, when it was under a minute ago. Lower case.

buildLog.ago.minutes_one.description: How long ago an app's deploy failed, in the "When:" line of the "Build log" panel. {{count}} is a number of minutes; "m" abbreviates minutes.

buildLog.ago.minutes_other.description: How long ago an app's deploy failed, in the "When:" line of the "Build log" panel. {{count}} is a number of minutes; "m" abbreviates minutes.

buildLog.ago.hours_one.description: How long ago an app's deploy failed, in the "When:" line of the "Build log" panel. {{count}} is a number of hours; "h" abbreviates hours.

buildLog.ago.hours_other.description: How long ago an app's deploy failed, in the "When:" line of the "Build log" panel. {{count}} is a number of hours; "h" abbreviates hours.

buildLog.ago.days_one.description: How long ago an app's deploy failed, in the "When:" line of the "Build log" panel. {{count}} is a number of days; "d" abbreviates days.

buildLog.ago.days_other.description: How long ago an app's deploy failed, in the "When:" line of the "Build log" panel. {{count}} is a number of days; "d" abbreviates days.

buildLog.ago.months_one.description: How long ago an app's deploy failed, in the "When:" line of the "Build log" panel. {{count}} is a number of months; "mo" abbreviates months.

buildLog.ago.months_other.description: How long ago an app's deploy failed, in the "When:" line of the "Build log" panel. {{count}} is a number of months; "mo" abbreviates months.

language.title.description: Heading of the Language section in Settings, where the person picks the language Homeroom is shown in. "Language" is a noun.

language.intro.text: The language Homeroom's screens are shown in. A language is listed once enough of Homeroom has been translated into it. Apps on Homeroom use your choice as their default, and some let you pick another in their own settings.
language.intro.description: Explanation under the Language heading in Settings: what choosing a language does, why a language may not be listed yet, and that apps follow it unless they offer their own choice.

language.auto.description: First option in the Language list in Settings: follow the language of the phone or browser instead of a fixed choice. Shown only for a moment, until the page knows which language that is.

language.autoCurrently.description: First option in the Language list in Settings: follow the language of the phone or browser instead of a fixed choice. {{language}} is the language that gives on this device, in its own name (for example "English" or "Español"), or English when Homeroom is not available in the device's language.

language.saved.description: Status line under the Language list in Settings after the choice was saved. Keep the check mark.

language.saveFailed.description: Status line under the Language list in Settings when the choice could not be saved and the server gave no reason.

language.loadFailed.text: Could not load that language. Try again.
language.loadFailed.description: Status line under the Language list in Settings when the chosen language's text could not be downloaded.

timezone.title.description: Heading of the Time zone section in Settings, under the Language section, where the person picks the time zone Homeroom shows times in.

timezone.intro.text: The time zone Homeroom uses for the times it shows you, on every device you sign in on. Auto follows this device's clock.
timezone.intro.description: Explanation under the Time zone heading in Settings: the choice is saved to the account, and Auto uses the phone's or computer's own time zone.

timezone.auto.description: First option in the Time zone list in Settings: follow the phone's or computer's own time zone. {{zone}} is that zone's name, for example "Europe / Paris".

timezone.saved.description: Status line under the Time zone list in Settings after the choice was saved. {{zone}} is the chosen zone's name, for example "America / New York", or the device's zone when Auto was chosen. Keep the check mark.

timezone.saveFailed.text: Could not save the time zone. Try again.
timezone.saveFailed.description: Status line under the Time zone list in Settings when the choice could not be saved (no connection, or the server refused it).

connectors.title.description: Heading of the Connectors section in Settings, where a person connects AI chat products (Claude, ChatGPT, Codex) to Homeroom.

connectors.intro.text: Work on your apps from a Claude or ChatGPT chat, without using your weekly credits.
connectors.intro.description: Explanation under the Connectors heading in Settings: what connecting a chat product is for. Claude and ChatGPT are product names.

connectors.url.label.description: Label of the read-only field in Settings > Connectors that holds the address to paste into the other product. "MCP" is the name of the standard and stays as is; the wording matches the field name in Claude and ChatGPT.

connectors.url.copyAria.description: Accessible name of the Copy button beside the MCP server URL field in Settings > Connectors.

connectors.test.button.description: Button beside Copy in Settings > Connectors. It checks this site's MCP server and the person's own connection, without connecting anything.

connectors.test.running.description: Label of the Test connection button in Settings > Connectors while the check runs. The button cannot be pressed again until it finishes.

connectors.test.unknownProduct.description: Fills the {{product}} slot in the passing lines under the Test connection button in Settings > Connectors when the connected chat product's name is not known. Lowercase, because it sits inside a sentence.

connectors.test.result.ok.text: Working: your MCP server answers and {{product}} is connected. If it still fails in {{product}}, go through its setup steps below again.
connectors.test.result.ok.description: Passing line under the Test connection button in Settings > Connectors when a chat product is connected and has never been used. {{product}} is the chat product's name (for example Claude.ai), taken from the Connected list below. MCP is the protocol name; keep it.

connectors.test.result.okUsed.text: Working: your MCP server answers and {{product}} is connected, last used {{lastUsed}}. If it still fails in {{product}}, go through its setup steps below again.
connectors.test.result.okUsed.description: Passing line under the Test connection button in Settings > Connectors when the chat product was used before. {{product}} is its name (for example Claude.ai); {{lastUsed}} is a date and time formatted the same way as in the Connected list below.

connectors.test.result.not_connected.text: Your MCP server works, but no chat product is connected yet. Choose your app below and follow its steps.
connectors.test.result.not_connected.description: Result under the Test connection button in Settings > Connectors when the server answers and the person has not connected a chat product yet.

connectors.test.result.connection_expire.text: Your MCP server works, but your connection has expired. Reconnect from your chat product, following its steps below.
connectors.test.result.connection_expire.description: Result under the Test connection button in Settings > Connectors when the person's connection exists but is no longer active.

connectors.test.result.unavailable_here.text: Connectors are not available on this copy of Homeroom. Use the Homeroom site at its usual address.
connectors.test.result.unavailable_here.description: Result under the Test connection button in Settings > Connectors on a preview copy of the site, where connecting a chat product is switched off.

connectors.test.result.discovery_failed.text: The sign-in details for the MCP server did not answer. This is on Homeroom's side: try again in a few minutes, and report it if it keeps happening.
connectors.test.result.discovery_failed.description: Result under the Test connection button in Settings > Connectors when the server's OAuth discovery metadata did not answer correctly. Homeroom is the product name; MCP is the protocol name.

connectors.test.result.server_unreachabl.text: The MCP server did not answer. This is on Homeroom's side: try again in a few minutes, and report it if it keeps happening.
connectors.test.result.server_unreachabl.description: Result under the Test connection button in Settings > Connectors when the MCP server itself did not answer. Homeroom is the product name; MCP is the protocol name.

connectors.test.result.test_failed.text: The test could not run. Check your internet connection and try again.
connectors.test.result.test_failed.description: Result under the Test connection button in Settings > Connectors when the check could not reach the site at all, for example because the person is offline.

connectors.howItWorks.summary.description: Tappable line under the MCP server URL field in Settings > Connectors: opens a short explanation of what the address is.

connectors.howItWorks.address.text: This is Homeroom’s address for AI apps. MCP is the standard they use to connect.
connectors.howItWorks.address.description: First paragraph of the "How it works" explanation in Settings > Connectors, about the MCP server URL above it. Homeroom is the product name; MCP stays as is.

connectors.howItWorks.paste.text: Paste it into Claude, ChatGPT or another app that supports MCP. That app can then see your Homeroom apps, file requests and open proposals for you.
connectors.howItWorks.paste.description: Second paragraph of the "How it works" explanation in Settings > Connectors. "It" is the MCP server URL. "file requests" and "open proposals" are verbs: the connected app can submit a change request or start a proposal on the person's behalf.

connectors.howItWorks.approve.text: You need no password or key. The app opens a Homeroom page, and you approve it there.
connectors.howItWorks.approve.description: Third paragraph of the "How it works" explanation in Settings > Connectors: how the other app gets permission. "The app" is the AI app being connected.

connectors.chooseApp.description: Small heading in Settings > Connectors above the cards, one card per AI tool (Claude.ai, ChatGPT, Codex, another agent), each with its status, its connections and its setup steps.

connectors.claude.hint.text: 6 steps · also sets up Claude Code
connectors.claude.hint.description: Second line of the Claude.ai row in the list of setup guides in Settings > Connectors: how long the guide is and what else it covers. The guide has exactly six steps. Claude Code is a product name.

connectors.chatgpt.hint.description: Small hint beside the ChatGPT heading of the foldable setup guide in Settings > Connectors: how many steps it has and where they happen (ChatGPT's plugins directory). Keep the middle dot.

connectors.codex.hint.description: Second line of the Codex row in the list of setup guides in Settings > Connectors. The guide has exactly three steps, done in a command-line terminal.

connectors.generic.title.description: Title of the last row in the list of setup guides in Settings > Connectors: instructions for any other AI coding agent that is not Claude, ChatGPT or Codex.

connectors.generic.hint.description: Second line of the "Another agent" row in Settings > Connectors. The guide has exactly four steps. An "MCP client" is any program that can connect to an MCP server.

connectors.guided.ask.description: Button at the top of a setup guide in Settings > Connectors: opens a new chat in that product which talks the person through setup. {{product}} is the product name, Claude or ChatGPT.

connectors.guided.opens.text: Opens a new {{product}} chat with your connector details already filled in.
connectors.guided.opens.description: Note under the "Ask … to guide you" button in Settings > Connectors. {{product}} is the product name, Claude or ChatGPT.

connectors.guided.orSteps.description: Small heading in a setup guide in Settings > Connectors, between the guided-chat button and the written numbered steps.

connectors.claudeCode.heading.description: Small heading inside the Claude.ai setup guide in Settings > Connectors, above two extra topics that only matter to people using the Claude Code product.

connectors.naming.title.description: Title of a row in the Claude.ai setup guide in Settings > Connectors: the connector must be given the name "homeroom". Keep "homeroom" in lower case, untranslated: it is the exact name to type.

connectors.naming.hint.description: Second line of the "Name it homeroom" row in Settings > Connectors: why the name matters. The rules are Claude Code permission rules that Homeroom ships.

connectors.naming.body.text: Name it exactly <0>homeroom</0>. Claude Code builds its permission rules from that name. A different spelling still works, but the read-only allowlist Homeroom ships in every app repo will not match it, and you will keep being asked to approve each call. The allowlist covers <1>Homeroom</1> as well, so the capitalised form is safe. It also still covers <2>usernode</2> and <3>Usernode</3>, the names this connector went by before, so a connector you added earlier keeps working and there is nothing to redo. Anything else needs the rules rewritten, which the field under “Stop the permission prompts” does for you.
connectors.naming.body.description: Body of the "Name it homeroom" row in Settings > Connectors. Explains which connector names the shipped permission rules cover. The quoted “Stop the permission prompts” is the title of the next row (settings:connectors.prompts.title) and must match it. Keep the text inside the numbered tags exactly as written: those are names and commands the reader types or looks for.

connectors.prompts.title.description: Title of a row in the Claude.ai setup guide in Settings > Connectors: how to stop Claude Code asking for approval before every connector call.

connectors.prompts.hint.text: If Claude Code asks before every call
connectors.prompts.hint.description: Second line of the "Stop the permission prompts" row in Settings > Connectors: when this topic applies.

connectors.prompts.intro.text: Claude Code asks you to approve <0>every</0> connector call by default, including read-only ones like <1>whoami</1> and <2>get_app</2>. Which fix applies depends on where you run it.
connectors.prompts.intro.description: First paragraph under "Stop the permission prompts" in Settings > Connectors. Tag 0 is emphasis on "every"; tags 1 and 2 are tool names and stay exactly as written.

connectors.prompts.ownership.text: Homeroom cannot switch this on for you. Permission rules live in a file on your machine or in your app’s repo, and a connector has no way to write either, which is also what stops any other connector you add from granting itself permissions. Copying one of the blocks below is the whole fix, and it is a one-time thing.
connectors.prompts.ownership.description: Second paragraph under "Stop the permission prompts" in Settings > Connectors: only the person can apply the fix, by copying one of the code blocks shown below it.

connectors.prompts.local.title.text: Claude Code on your own machine
connectors.prompts.local.title.description: Heading of the first of three cases under "Stop the permission prompts" in Settings > Connectors: Claude Code running on the person's own computer.

connectors.prompts.local.body.text: Add this to your own <0>~/.claude/settings.json</0>. It is the only one of the three that covers <1>every</1> repo at once, including repos Homeroom never made.
connectors.prompts.local.body.description: Text under "Claude Code on your own machine" in Settings > Connectors, above a block of settings to copy. Tag 0 is a file path and stays exactly as written; tag 1 is emphasis on "every". "The three" are the three cases listed in this section.

connectors.prompts.local.copyAria.text: Copy the allow rules for your personal settings file
connectors.prompts.local.copyAria.description: Accessible name of the Copy button above the first block of permission rules in Settings > Connectors, the one for the settings file on the person's own computer.

connectors.prompts.web.title.description: Heading of the second of three cases under "Stop the permission prompts" in Settings > Connectors: Claude Code running in the browser.

connectors.prompts.web.body.text: A web session gets a fresh container each time, so a settings file on your own machine is not in it and last session’s approvals are gone. What the container does carry is the repo it checks out, so commit the same block as <0>.claude/settings.json</0> in the app repo. Homeroom writes that file into every app repo it creates, imports or forks; repos that already existed before it shipped do not have one, and adding it is an ordinary commit.
connectors.prompts.web.body.description: Text under "Claude Code on the web" in Settings > Connectors, above a block of settings to copy. Tag 0 is a file path and stays exactly as written. "Commit" is the version-control verb.

connectors.prompts.web.copyAria.text: Copy the allow rules to commit in your app repo
connectors.prompts.web.copyAria.description: Accessible name of the Copy button above the second block of permission rules in Settings > Connectors, the one to commit into the app's code repository.

connectors.prompts.web.trust.text: Claude Code may still ask you to trust the workspace once per container before a repo-level file takes effect. Whether that dialog appears in every web session has not been settled. If you are still prompted after committing the file, that is the reason, and the case above is the fix that does not depend on it.
connectors.prompts.web.trust.description: Closing paragraph of the "Claude Code on the web" case in Settings > Connectors, under its block of rules. "The case above" is "Claude Code on your own machine".

connectors.prompts.chat.title.description: Heading of the third of three cases under "Stop the permission prompts" in Settings > Connectors. All three are product names.

connectors.prompts.chat.body.text: Nothing to do. You approve the connector once when you connect it and it does not ask again per call. The two blocks above are Claude Code’s file format and have no effect in those products.
connectors.prompts.chat.body.description: Text under "Claude.ai chat, ChatGPT and Codex" in Settings > Connectors: these products need no permission rules.

connectors.prompts.readsOnly.text: Reads only. Anything that acts on your behalf (filing a request, opening or advancing a proposal) still asks every time, on purpose.
connectors.prompts.readsOnly.description: Paragraph after the three cases under "Stop the permission prompts" in Settings > Connectors: the rules only silence prompts for calls that read data.

connectors.prompts.spelling.label.text: Connector registered under a different name?
connectors.prompts.spelling.label.description: Label of a text field at the end of "Stop the permission prompts" in Settings > Connectors, where the person types the name their connector actually has.

connectors.prompts.spelling.body.text: Check what your tools are called in your session, the middle part of <0>mcp__homeroom__whoami</0>. If it is not <1>homeroom</1>, <2>Homeroom</2>, <3>usernode</3> or <4>Usernode</4>, type it here and both blocks above are rewritten for it.
connectors.prompts.spelling.body.description: Help text between the "Connector registered under a different name?" label and its field in Settings > Connectors. Typing a name rewrites the two blocks of rules above. Keep the text inside the numbered tags exactly as written: those are names and commands the reader types or looks for.

connectors.codex.add.title.description: Step 1 of the Codex setup guide in Settings > Connectors, shown in bold at the start of the step's text. A complete sentence; the server is the Homeroom MCP server.

connectors.codex.add.body.text: From a terminal where Codex is installed, run the command below, or add the config entry below it to <0>~/.codex/config.toml</0> by hand, which is all the command does. Keep the name <1>homeroom</1>: Codex prefixes the tools with the server name you give it, and it is the name the rest of this page assumes.
connectors.codex.add.body.description: Text of step 1 ("Add the server.") of the Codex setup guide in Settings > Connectors. The command and the config entry are shown in two copyable blocks below the steps. Keep the text inside the numbered tags exactly as written: those are names and commands the reader types or looks for.

connectors.codex.signIn.title.description: Step 2 of the Codex setup guide in Settings > Connectors, shown in bold at the start of the step's text. An instruction to the reader.

connectors.codex.signIn.body.text: Run <0>codex mcp login homeroom</0>. Codex opens your browser on Homeroom’s consent page; approve it there and Codex keeps the token itself. There is no client ID or secret to enter. <1>codex mcp list</1> then shows the server, and the tools are there in your next Codex session.
connectors.codex.signIn.body.description: Text of step 2 ("Sign in.") of the Codex setup guide in Settings > Connectors. Tags 0 and 1 are commands to type and stay exactly as written.

connectors.codex.limit.title.description: Step 3 of the Codex setup guide in Settings > Connectors, shown in bold at the start of the step's text: introduces a current limitation.

connectors.codex.limit.body.text: Codex takes that approval on a <0>127.0.0.1</0> callback, and the hosted Homeroom connector accepts sign-in callbacks only on Claude’s and ChatGPT’s own hosts, so on the hosted platform the sign-in is refused with <1>invalid_redirect_uri</1>. It works against a Homeroom you run yourself in local-development mode. A Codex session without the connector can still build a Homeroom work order: it pushes the branch, and the ChatGPT chat that holds the connector submits it.
connectors.codex.limit.body.description: Text of step 3 ("Know the limit today.") of the Codex setup guide in Settings > Connectors: sign-in from Codex is refused on the hosted platform. Tag 0 is a network address and tag 1 an error code; both stay exactly as written. A "work order" is Homeroom's written hand-off for a coding agent.

connectors.codex.terminal.description: Small caption above the first copyable block in the Codex setup guide in Settings > Connectors: says the command below is typed in a command-line terminal. Lower case, like the file name shown above the second block.

connectors.codex.copyCommandAria.text: Copy the Codex command that adds the Homeroom server
connectors.codex.copyCommandAria.description: Accessible name of the Copy button above the terminal command in the Codex setup guide in Settings > Connectors.

connectors.codex.copyConfigAria.text: Copy the Codex config.toml entry for the Homeroom server
connectors.codex.copyConfigAria.description: Accessible name of the Copy button above the config file entry in the Codex setup guide in Settings > Connectors. config.toml is a file name and stays as is.

connectors.generic.transport.title.text: Give it the connector URL as a Streamable HTTP server.
connectors.generic.transport.title.description: Step 1 of the "Another agent" setup guide in Settings > Connectors, shown in bold at the start of the step's text. "It" is the agent being set up; "Streamable HTTP" is the name of an MCP transport and stays as is.

connectors.generic.transport.body.text: That is the URL in the field above: a public HTTPS endpoint ending in <0>/mcp</0> that takes JSON-RPC over POST. There is no SSE or stdio variant, and nothing to run on your own machine.
connectors.generic.transport.body.description: Text of step 1 of the "Another agent" setup guide in Settings > Connectors. Tag 0 is a URL path and stays exactly as written; JSON-RPC, POST, SSE and stdio are technical names.

connectors.generic.oauth.title.description: Step 2 of the "Another agent" setup guide in Settings > Connectors, shown in bold at the start of the step's text. "It" is the agent; OAuth is the sign-in standard.

connectors.generic.oauth.body.text: Auth is OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and dynamic client registration. A client finds the authorization server through <0>/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp</0> on the same origin, registers itself as a public client (no client ID or secret to enter), and asks for the scopes <1>usernode:apps:read</1> and <2>usernode:proposals:write</2>. You approve those once on Homeroom’s consent page.
connectors.generic.oauth.body.description: Text of step 2 of the "Another agent" setup guide in Settings > Connectors: how the agent signs in. Tag 0 is a URL path and tags 1 and 2 are permission scope names; all stay exactly as written.

connectors.generic.callback.title.description: Step 3 of the "Another agent" setup guide in Settings > Connectors, shown in bold at the start of the step's text. The callback is the address the agent's sign-in returns to.

connectors.generic.callback.body.text: Homeroom registers a client only if its OAuth callback is on <0>claude.ai</0>, <1>claude.com</1>, <2>chatgpt.com</2> or <3>openai.com</3> (or a host the deployment’s operator has added). A callback on localhost, which command-line clients use, is accepted only by a Homeroom running in local-development mode. A refused registration answers <4>invalid_redirect_uri</4>, and that is a limit on the platform side rather than something to fix in the client.
connectors.generic.callback.body.description: Text of step 3 of the "Another agent" setup guide in Settings > Connectors: which sign-in return addresses Homeroom accepts. Tags 0 to 3 are host names and tag 4 an error code; all stay exactly as written.

connectors.generic.naming.title.text: Name it homeroom and read your tool list.
connectors.generic.naming.title.description: Step 4 of the "Another agent" setup guide in Settings > Connectors, shown in bold at the start of the step's text. Keep "homeroom" in lower case, untranslated: it is the exact name to type.

connectors.generic.naming.body.text: Tools arrive as <0>mcp__homeroom__whoami</0> in most clients, or as <1>mcp__claude_ai_homeroom__whoami</1> where the client namespaces by product. The part between the first and last <2>__</2> is the server name the permission rules are written for; if it is not one of the spellings they cover, type it into the field under Claude.ai → “Stop the permission prompts”. Have the agent call <3>get_connector_guidance</3> first: it returns the connector’s full operating charter.
connectors.generic.naming.body.description: Text of step 4 of the "Another agent" setup guide in Settings > Connectors. The quoted “Stop the permission prompts” is a row title on this page (settings:connectors.prompts.title) and must match it; Claude.ai is the row it sits under. Keep the text inside the numbered tags exactly as written: those are names and commands the reader types or looks for.

connectors.approveNote.text: Whichever you use, approve the connection in the browser page that opens.
connectors.approveNote.description: Note under the list of setup guides in Settings > Connectors: applies to every product in the list.

connectors.list.disconnect.description: Button on a connection's row, on its AI tool's card in Settings > Connectors: removes that connection's access to Homeroom.

connectors.list.reconnect.description: Button under a connection whose sign-in ran out, on its AI tool's card in Settings > Connectors: opens that tool's setup steps at the one step that signs in again, so the person can connect it again without repeating the whole setup. Shown for Claude and Codex.

connectors.list.rename.description: Text button under a connection's lines, on its AI tool's card in Settings > Connectors: opens a small form under the row where the person types their own name for that connection (for example "Work laptop"), so two connections of the same tool can be told apart. A verb.

connectors.list.renameNamed.description: Screen-reader label of the Rename button on a connection's row in Settings > Connectors. {{name}} is the connection's current name: the person's own name for it, or the AI tool's name such as "Claude (claude.ai)". "Rename" is a verb.

connectors.claudeSteps.open.title.description: Step 1 of the Claude.ai connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Shown in bold at the start of the step's text; an instruction to the reader.

connectors.claudeSteps.open.body.text: Go to <0>Customize → Connectors</0> in Claude (<1>claude.ai/customize/connectors</1>). This is where both directory connectors and your own custom ones live.
connectors.claudeSteps.open.body.description: Text of step 1 of the Claude.ai connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Tag 0 is a menu path in Claude's own interface (use Claude's wording in the target language if it differs); tag 1 is a web address and stays exactly as written.

connectors.claudeSteps.start.title.description: Step 2 of the Claude.ai connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Shown in bold at the start of the step's text; an instruction to the reader.

connectors.claudeSteps.start.body.text: Click the <0>+</0> button, then choose “Add custom connector”. In the dialog, put <1>homeroom</1> in the Name field, exactly that spelling: Claude Code builds its permission rules from what you type here, and the read-only allowlist Homeroom ships in every app repo matches only the names it knows. On Team or Enterprise plans this option isn’t there for members, so an Owner adds it first from Organization settings → Connectors (Add → hover “Custom” → “Web”).
connectors.claudeSteps.start.body.description: Text of step 2 of the Claude.ai connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Tag 0 is the plus sign on a button; tag 1 is the exact name to type and stays "homeroom". The quoted words are labels in Claude's own interface.

connectors.claudeSteps.paste.title.description: Step 3 of the Claude.ai connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Shown in bold at the start of the step's text; an instruction to the reader.

connectors.claudeSteps.paste.body.text: For Homeroom that is the MCP server URL above, a public HTTPS endpoint ending in <0>/mcp</0>. A custom server must be reachable from Anthropic’s cloud, not just from your machine.
connectors.claudeSteps.paste.body.description: Text of step 3 of the Claude.ai connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. "The MCP server URL above" is a field shown above the steps. Tag 0 is a URL ending and stays exactly as written. Anthropic is the company that makes Claude.

connectors.claudeSteps.oauth.title.description: Step 4 of the Claude.ai connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Shown in bold at the start of the step's text; an instruction to the reader.

connectors.claudeSteps.oauth.body.text: If a server requires OAuth, open “Advanced settings” and enter your OAuth Client ID and Client Secret. Skip this for Homeroom: it uses dynamic client registration, so there is nothing to enter.
connectors.claudeSteps.oauth.body.description: Text of step 4 of the Claude.ai connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps: this step can be skipped for Homeroom. The quoted words and "Client ID", "Client Secret" are labels in Claude's own interface.

connectors.claudeSteps.save.title.description: Step 5 of the Claude.ai connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Shown in bold at the start of the step's text; an instruction to the reader.

connectors.claudeSteps.save.body.text: Click “Add” to finish configuring, then click “Connect” next to the connector. You’ll be redirected through the OAuth flow; review the scopes it asks for before approving.
connectors.claudeSteps.save.body.description: Text of step 5 of the Claude.ai connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. “Add” and “Connect” are buttons in Claude's own interface. "Scopes" are the permissions the connection asks for.

connectors.claudeSteps.enable.title.description: Step 6 of the Claude.ai connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Shown in bold at the start of the step's text. "It" is the connector; a conversation is a chat in Claude.

connectors.claudeSteps.enable.body.text: In a chat, use the <0>+</0> button at the lower left, then “Connectors”, and toggle your connector on. Toggles are per-conversation, so you control which chats can reach it.
connectors.claudeSteps.enable.body.description: Text of step 6 of the Claude.ai connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Tag 0 is the plus sign on a button; “Connectors” is a menu item in Claude's own interface.

connectors.chatgptSteps.directory.title.description: Step 1 of the ChatGPT connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Shown in bold at the start of the step's text; an instruction to the reader. The plugins directory is a page of ChatGPT.

connectors.chatgptSteps.directory.body.text: Go to <0>chatgpt.com/plugins</0> in your browser. Plugin and MCP setup is currently a web feature.
connectors.chatgptSteps.directory.body.description: Text of step 1 of the ChatGPT connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. <0></0> is a link to that address; keep the address as it is. MCP is the name of the protocol connectors use.

connectors.chatgptSteps.create.title.description: Step 2 of the ChatGPT connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Shown in bold at the start of the step's text; an instruction to the reader. MCP is a protocol name.

connectors.chatgptSteps.create.body.text: Click <0>“Add plugin”</0>, then choose <1>“Create custom MCP server”</1>.
connectors.chatgptSteps.create.body.description: Text of step 2 of the ChatGPT connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. The two quoted names are buttons in ChatGPT's own interface, drawn in bold; write them as ChatGPT shows them in the reader's language if known, otherwise keep the English.

connectors.chatgptSteps.url.title.description: Step 3 of the ChatGPT connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Shown in bold at the start of the step's text; the address to enter is shown right after it. Homeroom is the product's name.

connectors.chatgptSteps.use.title.text: Turn the server on in a chat.
connectors.chatgptSteps.use.title.description: Step 4 of the ChatGPT connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. Shown in bold at the start of the step's text; an instruction to the reader. The server is the MCP server just created.

connectors.chatgptSteps.use.body.text: Open the <0>+</0> / connector picker next to the message box, select the server you just created, and set it as active. Now ask ChatGPT to perform something that uses one of the tools, for example: <1>“Use my MCP server to list the open support tickets.”</1> When appropriate, ChatGPT will call the tools your MCP server exposes and use their results in the conversation.
connectors.chatgptSteps.use.body.description: Text of step 4 of the ChatGPT connector setup steps, shown in Settings > Connectors and in a new thread's setup steps. <0></0> holds the plus sign that is on the button; keep it. <1></1> is an example request in italics.

connectors.chatgptSteps.inShort.text: <0>In short:</0> chatgpt.com/plugins → Add plugin → Create custom MCP server → enter the Homeroom MCP server URL → connector picker → set it active.
connectors.chatgptSteps.inShort.description: Summary line under the ChatGPT connector setup steps: the same steps as a chain. <0></0> is the bold lead-in. Keep the arrows and the address; "Add plugin" and "Create custom MCP server" are button names in ChatGPT.

linkedAccounts.title.description: Heading of the Linked accounts section in Settings, where a person connects a GitHub or X account to raise their weekly AI credits.

linkedAccounts.intro.text: We pay for these credits, so a connected account helps us stop one person making many.
linkedAccounts.intro.description: Explanation under the Linked accounts heading in Settings: why connecting a GitHub or X account raises weekly credits. "Making many" means making many Homeroom accounts.

linkedAccounts.scope.text: Homeroom asks for<0> no access to your repositories </0>and stores no provider token. Connecting confirms you control the account. It is not proof of unique humanity.
linkedAccounts.scope.description: Note under the list of linked accounts in Settings: what connecting a GitHub or X account does and does not give Homeroom. Tag 0 is bold. The spaces just inside the tag are the only spaces around those words, so keep one on each side, inside the tag.

linkedAccounts.dailyCredits.description: Small heading above the list in Settings > Linked accounts that shows the person's weekly AI credit level and the accounts that raise it.

linkedAccounts.auditNote.text: Review or revoke this authorization at <0>{{address}}</0>.
linkedAccounts.auditNote.description: Line in an opened GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts. Tag 0 is a link to the provider's own page of authorized apps; {{address}} is that page's web address as text, for example github.com/settings/applications.

linkedAccounts.showOnProfile.description: Label of a switch in an opened GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts: whether the linked account is shown on the person's public Homeroom profile.

linkedAccounts.disconnect.description: Button in an opened GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts: unlinks that account from the Homeroom account.

linkedAccounts.status.openingBrowser.description: Status line under a GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts, in the phone app, while the system browser is being opened to connect the account.

linkedAccounts.status.finishConnecting.text: Finish connecting in your browser, then return to the app. Sign in with the same Homeroom account if asked.
linkedAccounts.status.finishConnecting.description: Status line under a GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts, in the phone app, after the browser opened to connect an account for the first time.

linkedAccounts.status.finishVerification.text: Finish verification in your browser, then return to the app. Sign in with the same Homeroom account if asked.
linkedAccounts.status.finishVerification.description: Status line under a GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts, in the phone app, after the browser opened to re-verify or change an already linked account.

linkedAccounts.status.savingVisibility.description: Status line under a GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts while the "Show on public profile" switch is being saved.

linkedAccounts.status.visibilityFailed.description: Error under a GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts when the "Show on public profile" switch could not be saved and the server gave no reason.

linkedAccounts.status.shownOnProfile.description: Status line under a GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts after the linked account was made visible on the person's public profile.

linkedAccounts.status.hiddenFromProfile.description: Status line under a GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts after the linked account was hidden from the person's public profile.

linkedAccounts.status.replacing.description: Status line under a GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts while the linked account is being swapped for the newly verified one.

linkedAccounts.status.replaceFailed.description: Error under a GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts when swapping the linked account failed and the server gave no reason.

linkedAccounts.status.replaced.description: Status line under a row in Settings > Linked accounts after the linked account was swapped for another. {{provider}} is GitHub or X.

linkedAccounts.status.cancelFailed.description: Error under a GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts when cancelling a pending account swap failed and the server gave no reason.

linkedAccounts.status.replacementCancell.text: No changes made. @{{handle}} is still connected.
linkedAccounts.status.replacementCancell.description: Status line under a GitHub or X row in Settings > Linked accounts after the person cancelled a pending account swap. {{handle}} is the user name of the account that stays linked; keep the @ before it.

linkedAccounts.replacement.aria.description: Accessible name of the confirmation card in Settings > Linked accounts that asks whether to swap the linked account for a newly verified one. {{provider}} is GitHub or X.

linkedAccounts.replacement.title.description: Title of the confirmation card in Settings > Linked accounts that asks whether to swap the linked account for a newly verified one. {{provider}} is GitHub or X.

linkedAccounts.replacement.intro.text: The new account is verified. Nothing changes until you confirm.
linkedAccounts.replacement.intro.description: Text under the title of the account replacement card in Settings > Linked accounts.

linkedAccounts.replacement.current.description: Small caption over the user name of the account that is linked now, on the left of the account replacement card in Settings > Linked accounts. Adjective: the current account.

linkedAccounts.replacement.verified.description: Small caption over the user name of the new account, on the right of the account replacement card in Settings > Linked accounts. Noun: the replacement account, already verified.

linkedAccounts.replacement.showOnProfile.text: Show the replacement on my public profile
linkedAccounts.replacement.showOnProfile.description: Label of a switch on the account replacement card in Settings > Linked accounts: whether the new account will be shown on the person's public profile.

linkedAccounts.replacement.cancelNote.text: Cancelling keeps @{{handle}} connected with its current visibility.
linkedAccounts.replacement.cancelNote.description: Note above the buttons of the account replacement card in Settings > Linked accounts. {{handle}} is the user name of the account linked now; keep the @ before it.

linkedAccounts.replacement.confirm.description: Button on the account replacement card in Settings > Linked accounts: confirms swapping the linked account for the newly verified one.

linkedAccounts.replacement.replacing.description: Label of the "Replace account" button in Settings > Linked accounts while the swap is in progress.

linkedAccounts.diagnostics.summary.description: Tappable line under a row in Settings > Linked accounts, shown only to platform administrators: opens technical details of how sign-in with that provider is configured. {{provider}} is GitHub or X.

linkedAccounts.diagnostics.callbackUri.description: Label before a web address in the administrators-only setup panel in Settings > Linked accounts: the return address that must be registered with the provider. Keep the colon.

linkedAccounts.diagnostics.run.description: Button in the administrators-only setup panel in Settings > Linked accounts: tests whether the provider accepts the platform's credentials. "Run" is a verb.

linkedAccounts.diagnostics.checking.description: Line beside the "Run configuration check" button in Settings > Linked accounts while the check is in progress.

linkedAccounts.diagnostics.accepted.text: {{provider}} accepted the platform’s client credentials. If connecting still fails on {{provider}}’s own page, the callback address above is not registered on the {{provider}} app.
